items.english: Because of typhoon number eight, the express train might be late
items.korean: 팔 호 태풍 때문에 특급 열차가 늦을 수도 있어요
items.input: Because of typhoon number eight, the express train might be late

target.korean: 팔 호 태풍 때문에 특급 열차가 늦을 수도 있어요
target.natural_english: Because of typhoon number eight, the express train might be late
target.literal_gap: 늦을 수도 있어요 presents lateness as one possible outcome. The literal possibility-exists construction with 도 therefore becomes “might be late,” not the train’s ability or intention to arrive late.

items.sourceNote: The might standing alone, closing the sentence: 늦을 수도 있어요 — M8's 늦다 on the prospective badge, 수, 도, 있다 — says only that lateness is not ruled out; 늦을 거예요 would bet on it, 늦겠어요 would read it off the sky. The reason is the OTHER 때문: M29's 때문 in its noun job, straight on 태풍 (M11), no -기 needed because a typhoon is already a noun — the radar this module's Part 3 draws. 팔 호 labels the storm the way the news does (M2's 팔 in front of 호), and 특급 열차 stacks two grades: the top-rank train on M50's 열차, which even a typhoon can only maybe delay.

sourceGap.note: Korean builds 'can' out of existence: 수 is a way/means, so ability = 'the way exists' and inability = 'the way doesn't exist' (갈 수 없어요). The same 있다/없다 factory that built 맛있다 and 재미있다 — existence is Korean's favorite raw material.

items.english: She answered quietly, smiling

target.natural_english: She answered quietly, smiling
target.literal_gap: 그녀 combines the written elements that and woman to function as “she.” In this sentence it refers back to the woman answering; it is not a fresh instruction to identify “that woman” by pointing.

items.sourceNote: The novel's line: 웃으며 — M7's 웃다 on -(으)며, the written twin of -(으)면서 from M38 (its md rule, 'One subject does both things', holds here: one face smiles and answers). Consonant stem, so 으며; 웃으면서 would be the same sentence said aloud. 그녀 is the pronoun print invented for exactly this sentence — the mouth would say 그 사람은 or her name — and M33's 조용히 sits just before the closer, M10's 대답하다. Read it in a novel; never hear it in a kitchen.

sourceGap.natural: the 'she' Korean built for print in the early twentieth century — read on every page of every novel, said aloud by nobody
sourceGap.note: This module's 그녀 is younger than the grandmothers who read it: Korean had no separate 'she' until novelists of the 1920s, translating and imitating Japanese fiction, copied 彼女 (that-woman) character for character — M29's 그 + the 女 of M4's 여자 — to give their heroines a pronoun. Before that, prose used 그 for anyone, and it still does for men; 그녀 is the only gendered pronoun the language owns, and it never crossed into the mouth. Say 그녀 in conversation and you sound like a subtitle; the mouth points (그 사람, M55's 걔) or names (M4's 씨). The complaint that it is a Japanese import and should be retired surfaces every decade, and every decade the novels keep it. A word that shows what the written register is: not older Korean, but a Korean built for the page.

items.english: No matter how fierce the competition is, you must not give up on cooperation
items.korean: 아무리 경쟁이 심하더라도 협력을 포기하면 안 돼요
items.input: No matter how fierce the competition is, you must not give up on cooperation

target.korean: 아무리 경쟁이 심하더라도 협력을 포기하면 안 돼요
target.natural_english: No matter how fierce the competition is, you must not give up on cooperation
target.literal_gap: 포기하면 안 돼요 literally says that giving up will not do. It is a prohibition against abandoning cooperation despite competition, not a prediction that abandoning it cannot happen.

items.sourceNote: -더라도 on its debut, with the adverb that announces it: M39's 아무리 — that note's "the -아/어도 amplifier" — now amplifying the firmer rung. 경쟁이 심하더라도 (M39's 심하다) = even if the competition is severe, and 심해도 would say the same thing with less spine; the -더- inside is the retrospective syllable of M88, pointing at a scene the speaker has not yet lived but is willing to imagine. Then the veto every learner owns: 포기하면 안 돼요 — M35's 포기하다 in -(으)면 from M20 with 안 돼요 from M10, the must-not frame the M20 md built. Today's 경쟁 and 협력 stand on the two sides of the concession: the war with running, and the joined strength that answers it.

sourceGap.note: 되다 means become-work-be-okay, so its negation is the universal veto: rules (여기서 사진 안 돼요 — no photos here), refusals, and pure disbelief. Screamed without the 요 — 안 돼!!! — it's the sound of every K-drama's worst moment.

target.korean: 총리는 기자 회견에서 성명을 발표하며 정치권에 강한 경고를 보냈습니다
target.natural_english: The prime minister issued a statement at a press conference and sent a strong warning to the political class
target.literal_gap: 기자 회견 literally combines reporters with a meeting. As a fixed expression it names a press conference, so the statement is made at that event rather than at an unspecified meeting with an individual reporter.

items.sourceNote: Recycles -(으)며 from M85 — the written and/while, which that md sorted by one test: "one body doing two things = while; two facts side by side = and". Here one body: 발표하며 is M16's 발표하다 with 며 on its vowel stem — the prime minister issued the statement AND, in the same breath, sent the warning; aloud it would be 발표하면서, with -(으)면서 from M38, and the newsreader is the only mouth that says 며. sourceGap.natural: a press conference — the room where the statement is read and the questions are not always answered

items.english: What the so-called experts say in the end amounts to corporate PR
items.korean: 소위 전문가들의 말은 결국 기업 홍보인 셈이에요
items.input: What the so-called experts say in the end amounts to corporate PR

target.korean: 소위 전문가들의 말은 결국 기업 홍보인 셈이에요
target.natural_english: What the so-called experts say in the end amounts to corporate PR
target.literal_gap: 소위 marks “experts” as a label being questioned. English “so-called” preserves the skepticism supported by the later criticism of corporate PR; a neutral translation as merely experts would lose that stance.

items.sourceNote: Recycles -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 from M87 — the reckoning shelf, where that md glossed 셈이다 as "it amounts to" — on its noun row: 홍보인 셈이에요, the copula's 인 badge on today's 홍보, then M87's 셈. It does not say the experts are PR; it counts up what they said and finds that the total is PR, which is the columnist's favourite arithmetic. Two of today's words open it: 소위 puts the tongs on M58's 전문가 (with the plural -들 from M27 and the possessive 의), and 기업 홍보 (M90's 기업 + 홍보) is what the sum comes to; M32's 결국 does the adding, and M4's 말 on 은 is the subject the whole sentence weighs. Said, not printed — 셈이에요 in the 요 register — because this is the reader at breakfast, talking back to the page.

sourceGap.natural: so-called — the columnist's scare quotes, in one word
sourceGap.note: Today's 소위 before a noun does what English does with two raised fingers: 소위 전문가 (M58's 전문가) — the 'experts'; 소위 명문대 — the 'top' universities; 소위 선진국 (M97's 선진국) — the 'developed' world. The word claims only that the noun is what people CALL it, and the eyebrow supplies the rest. It is print-only: aloud, Koreans reach for 이른바 (riding frozen — the native twin, warmer, and just as skeptical) or for the plain 말하는, or they simply pause. Rule of thumb for a reader: a 소위 in an editorial means the writer disagrees with the noun; a 소위 in a report means the writer is quoting a label they did not choose. Either way the quotation marks are already there — do not add a second pair.
